title: Israel's memorial and independence days
hook: Yom HaZikaron honors the fallen, then Yom HaAtzmaut follows; communities worldwide mark them very differently, and some not at all

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yom HaShoah: candles, a siren and names. Your line was remember in silence. Did you find two minutes for it? A week later come two more days, side by side. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

Imagine a country where the saddest day of the year and the happiest day of the year are separated by a single sunset. In the morning, families stand at military cemeteries, by the graves of sons and daughters, brothers, parents. A siren stops traffic. The radio plays only quiet songs. And then, as evening comes, in one ceremony, the flag is raised from half-mast, torches are lit, and fireworks go up. Many of the same people who stood at the graves that morning are at a barbecue the next afternoon. The calendar puts them back to back on purpose.
screen: `THE SADDEST DAY, THEN THE HAPPIEST.` → `ONE SUNSET BETWEEN THEM.` → `BACK TO BACK, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The first day is Yom HaZikaron, the day of remembrance, on the fourth of the Hebrew month of Iyar. It honors Israel's fallen soldiers, and in more recent decades, civilians killed in attacks. A siren sounds in the evening, and again the next morning. Almost every family in the country knows someone on the list. The second day is Yom HaAtzmaut, Independence Day, on the fifth of Iyar. It marks the declaration of the State of Israel in May 1948. When either day would touch Shabbat, the dates are moved. The move from one to the other is the point: the state's founders tied them together, so that celebration never forgets its cost. Memory first, then celebration. Outside Israel, and within it, Jews mark these days very differently. Many communities hold memorial services and festive gatherings; some add prayers, and many religious Zionists recite the psalms of praise called Hallel on Independence Day. Many Reform and Conservative congregations have added readings for it. Many Haredi communities don't mark the days as religious occasions, and a few Haredi groups oppose the state on religious grounds. Many secular Israelis celebrate with no prayers at all, just flags and picnics. And for Palestinians, the same events of 1948 are remembered as the Nakba, the catastrophe, marked in mid-May. Today we're not asking which view is right. We're learning what's there: a pair of days, one of grief and one of joy, and a world of Jews who hold them in many different ways, and some who hold them not at all.
screen: `YOM HAZIKARON: THE FALLEN.` · `YOM HAATZMAUT: MAY 1948.` · `ONE SUNSET BETWEEN THEM.` · `MANY WAYS, AND SOME NOT AT ALL.` · then, large: `MEMORY BEFORE CELEBRATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn how one community marks them. Before the bell, breathe, and think of a community you know, or could find out about: your own synagogue, a friend's family, a city in Israel, a community abroad. What might they do on these two days? Make a note to ask, or to read, today. Then sit with the shape of the days themselves: grief, a sunset, then joy. Think of a time in your own life when a loss and a celebration came close together. The bell holds the time.
Israel's memorial and independence days. Yom HaZikaron, then Yom HaAtzmaut: remembrance, then celebration, a sunset apart. Today's word.
screen: `ISRAEL'S MEMORIAL AND INDEPENDENCE DAYS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: memory before celebration. Today, before you celebrate anything, even something small, take a moment to remember what it cost someone. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: In Israel, Yom HaZikaron is marked with sirens and ceremonies at military cemeteries, and Yom HaAtzmaut begins at nightfall with a torch-lighting ceremony; Jewish communities elsewhere mark the days in many ways, some with added prayers such as Hallel, and some not at all.
